text.title: Facilitation Anti-Patterns Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules with rationale + source for facilitation-anti-patterns. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: If the sponsor speaks for more than five consecutive minutes inside an elicitation block, the BA interrupts with a written-poll round (sticky notes or chat) addressed to every other participant by name.
rule.rationale: Past a few minutes of uninterrupted senior speech the room switches from elicitation to audience mode, and the silence that follows is read by the sponsor as agreement. A written poll addressed to people by name breaks the mode without contradicting the sponsor in public: it collects positions that would otherwise never be voiced, and nobody has to interrupt a superior out loud to give one.

rule.statement: Before any 'are we agreed?' close, the BA explicitly asks 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong?' and waits at least 15 seconds of silence before accepting the agreement.
rule.rationale: Are we agreed is a question that costs nothing to answer yes to and something to answer no to, so it reliably returns yes. Asking what would have to be true for this to be wrong reframes the social act from opposing the group to helping it stress-test, which is safe to do aloud. The silence is part of the mechanism, since objections take longer to formulate than agreement and an early close collects only the fast answers.

rule.statement: For every new question, every participant writes their answer privately for 90 seconds before any verbal sharing; the BA only reveals contributions after collection.
rule.rationale: The first answer spoken sets the frame for every answer after it, because later contributors respond to that answer rather than to the question, and genuinely different framings are never stated. Private writing before sharing is the only reliable way to collect independent positions, and it also protects the participants who need time to compose and would otherwise never get the floor.

rule.statement: Every parking-lot item is tagged with an owner and a 'review by' timestamp inside the same session; any item older than two cycles without a decision is auto-escalated to the sponsor with a 'kill or schedule' choice — never silently dropped.
rule.rationale: The parking lot is a socially acceptable way to defer a disagreement, so items land there precisely because they are contentious. With no owner and no review time it becomes the graveyard of every hard question in the engagement, and those questions come back as change requests during delivery. An escalation carrying an explicit kill-or-schedule choice forces the decision from the only person able to make it.

rule.statement: When the highest-paid person in the room overrides a workshop position, the BA writes the override into the minutes as 'decision by authority' with the named decider, the rejected alternatives, and the reason given — never as 'the group decided'.
rule.rationale: Recording an override as a group decision is a false record with a delayed cost: when it goes wrong, the people who argued against it are held accountable for it, and the same override recurs because nothing in the minutes shows it was ever contested. Naming the decider and the rejected alternatives leaves the authority intact, since the sponsor may still decide, while preserving the reasoning needed to revisit it later.

rule.statement: If the conversation drifts off the published agenda for more than ten minutes, the BA stops and asks the room: 're-contract to the new topic and drop X, or park this and return to X?' — the room must vote before continuing.
rule.rationale: Drift is usually not noise; it is the room discovering that a different question is more urgent. The failure is doing both badly: the new topic gets half a session with no preparation, and the displaced agenda item is silently dropped yet reported as covered. Making the room choose explicitly means whichever topic loses is known to have lost and can be rescheduled.

rule.statement: If the workshop has no power asymmetry, no contractual deliverable, and no historical anti-pattern, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Every counter-move here trades session time for protection against a specific pressure: authority distorting the record, or a contested position being lost. In a peer group producing nothing contractual that pressure is absent, and silent writes, forced dissent and minuted overrides read as procedural distrust of colleagues, which costs more in willingness to participate than it buys in fidelity.
